summary:
Genesis 5 records the generations from Adam to Noah. At first glance the chapter may seem like a simple list of names and numbers, but its repeated pattern carries a deeper message. Again and again the passage ends with the same words: "and he died." This steady rhythm reminds the reader that the consequence God warned about in Eden has now entered the world. Death has become part of the human story.

Yet the chapter also reveals that God's purpose for humanity continues. Adam's descendants are described as being born "in his likeness, according to his image," echoing the language of Genesis 1. Even after the fall, the image of God continues through human generations.

One life interrupts the pattern—Enoch. Instead of the words "and he died," the text says that Enoch walked with God, and God took him. This brief moment stands out like a light in the middle of the chapter, reminding the reader that fellowship with God is still possible even in a fallen world.

The genealogy eventually leads to Noah, whose birth brings hope that relief might come from the painful toil that began after the curse. Genesis 5 quietly moves the story forward, showing both the spread of death and the preservation of God's plan through generations.
